subcategory: specialty vine fruit / natural sweetener crop

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or grafted plants after all frost danger has passed on a sturdy trellis in full sun; give the shallow, brittle root system consistent moisture and a thick mulch layer through the long, hot growing season.

directions: Grow this dioecious perennial vine on a strong arbor or fence, planting at least one male vine for every six to eight female vines to ensure fruit set. The round green fruits, picked in autumn and dried, contain mogrosides that make them intensely sweet with none of the calories of sugar, and gardeners in zone 8-10 areas often treat the vine as a cut-back perennial that resprouts from the crown after light winter dieback. It prefers rich, well-drained soil high in organic matter and benefits from the same humid summer heat that suits muscadine grapes. Home use is mainly for steeping into tea or extracting a home sweetener rather than fresh eating, since the raw fruit is bitter until dried and cured.
sources: University of Kentucky Center for Crop Diversification

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in full sun well after the soil has warmed past last frost; in zone 9a treat as a large container specimen that can be moved under cover, since mature wood is damaged by hard freezes.

directions: This extremely fast-growing pioneer tree bears small, soft, cotton-candy-sweet red berries almost continuously in warm weather, often fruiting within its first year or two from seed. It tolerates poor soil and drought once established but is reliably hardy only in zone 10-11, so Gulf Coast growers farther north typically grow it in a large pot that can be sheltered indoors during freeze events. Fruit is eaten fresh, dropping by the handful onto the ground when ripe, and it draws strong bird and wildlife interest, making it a useful fast-establishing pollinator and wildlife planting in warm-climate food forests.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

planting.note: Plant grafted or own-root stock in spring in full sun on well-drained soil; this thorny shrubby citrus handles both Gulf Coast heat and brief hard freezes far better than typical lime cultivars.

directions: Native to the semi-arid interior of Australia, this small-fruited citrus relative is among the most cold-hardy true citrus species available, tolerating brief dips into the high teens Fahrenheit once established, which makes it a worthwhile dooryard planting for zone 9a gardeners where standard limes struggle. The pea-to-marble-sized round fruits have a tart, intensely aromatic lime flavor and are used in marmalades, cordials, and as a lime substitute; the species is also valued by citrus breeders as rootstock and hybrid parent material for cold tolerance. Give it excellent drainage and minimal supplemental water once established, since it is adapted to low-rainfall conditions and resents wet feet more than most citrus.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Citrus Program
Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

planting.note: Grow only in the mildest zone 9-11 microclimates or in a large protected container, planting in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; young trees need frost protection for their first several winters.

directions: This large subtropical tree, widely cultivated across southern China and Southeast Asia, produces olive-shaped drupes with an edible oily, nut-like kernel inside fibrous flesh that is traditionally pickled, candied, or cooked rather than eaten raw off the tree. It is unrelated to the Mediterranean olive but fills a similar culinary role in Chinese cuisine, where preserved and salted fruits are a common snack. Because it is only reliably hardy to around 25-28°F, treat it as an experimental planting for the warmest, most sheltered Gulf Coast sites, and expect a long juvenile period of many years before first fruiting from seed-grown trees.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops & Plant Products

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into rich, humus-heavy woodland soil under deciduous trees; the deep taproot resents disturbance, so choose a permanent spot and be patient while the clump establishes.

directions: This diminutive European woodland perennial in the carrot family produces odd, charming chartreuse flowers ringed by leaf-like bracts in very early spring, often before the surrounding trees have leafed out, followed by neatly lobed dark-green leaves that persist as a low mound through summer. It is slow to bulk up from seed or division but extremely long-lived and undemanding once settled, forming a slowly expanding clump that needs almost no maintenance. Use it as a specimen at the front of a shaded border or rock garden alongside other early bloomers like hellebores or snowdrops; it resents hot, dry summers and is best suited to cool woodland conditions rather than the Deep South.

planting.note: Plant divisions in early spring into consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in a shaded woodland or streamside setting; established clumps can be split every few years to propagate more plants.

directions: Close relative of the ornamental royal fern, this East Asian species is grown specifically for its edible spring fiddleheads, which emerge wrapped in distinctive rusty-brown wool and are harvested young, then parboiled and soaked to remove bitterness before use in Japanese and Korean cooking as zenmai. Leave most fronds on the plant to mature into tall, upright fertile and sterile fronds that provide good textural contrast through summer and clean yellow fall color. It thrives in the same moist, humus-rich, part-to-full-shade conditions as other Osmunda species and resents drying out, making it a good fit for rain gardens or pond edges.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
